scenes.headline: How a video model learns to move a robot arm
scenes.sub: Praxis-1 reads motion off a future it is still imagining
scenes.say: Hi, I'm Wystan! Praxis-1 is Runway's open-weight robot policy. Here's how a video model ends up driving an arm.

scenes.title: Three ways to drive an arm
scenes.say: Chapter one. Three ways to drive an arm.

scenes.title: Three families of robot policy
scenes.say: A robot policy maps what it sees to a short chunk of motion. Three families compete.

items.say: A vision-language-action model starts from a language model. It knows what a comb is, not how it moves when pushed.
A world model predicts the scene given an action. It is a simulator. It does not act.
A world action model predicts frames and actions together. The bet: weights that imagine the scene learn the motion. And video is cheap.

scenes.title: Inside the 54.4 GB
scenes.sub: A video backbone, a small expert, thin per-robot projections
scenes.say: Chapter two. Inside the fifty-four gigabytes.

steps.term: Mixture of experts: each token uses 8 of 128
steps.say: Runway's figure. A video backbone of fourteen encoder blocks, mostly mixture of experts: twenty-six point nine billion parameters, two point eight billion active.
Below it, the action expert: sixteen layers, three hundred and fourteen million parameters. Every other layer is a cross-attention.
Each reads one tapped encoder block, along these dotted lines.
Each call takes an instruction, the latest frames from two cameras, and where the arm is right now.
A mixture-of-experts video model starts denoising the next stretch of video.

steps.note: nothing flows back into the video model
steps.say: A small action expert taps eight of its layers, reading the future as the backbone imagines it. Nothing flows back.
Out come twenty-four rows of motion: one point six seconds at fifteen hertz.

steps.term: Chunk: 1.6 s of motion, then look again
steps.say: Time is cut into chunks of one point six seconds. The exterior and wrist cameras sit side by side on one canvas.
A frozen video autoencoder shrinks it sixteen times in each direction.
Two by two patches make a hundred and eighty-two tokens per latent frame.
Six latent frames: one thousand and ninety-two video tokens per chunk.
The expert holds just fifteen tokens. The arm's motion is a rounding error in the sequence.
Who reads what. Each row is one chunk's actions. They read the global tokens, and clean copies of the chunks before them.
And the diagonal: the backbone's noised version of the very chunk being acted on. The actions read the future as the backbone imagines it.

scenes.title: Two steps, unfinished video
scenes.sub: What the shipped sampler actually does
scenes.say: Chapter three. Two steps, and a video it never finishes.

scenes.text: The robot's next 1.6 seconds of motion are read off the backbone while its picture of those seconds is still almost pure noise.
scenes.say: Here's the surprise in the code. The next one point six seconds of motion are read off the backbone while its picture of them is still almost pure noise.

scenes.title: Two steps, on a toy reach

params.actions: toy: 24 rows of reach, two mugs, 50/50
legend: Shift 12.5 squeezes the middle call up to 0.926
t = 1: video and actions are pure noise
Step one: the video moves 7.4% of the way
Step two: actions jump to clean, the decoder is skipped
8 steps: the reach commits to one mug

steps.say: Sampling walks time from one, pure noise, to zero, clean. The served config takes two steps and shifts the grid by twelve point five, so the middle call lands at zero point nine two six.
Both the video and the actions start as pure noise.

steps.term: Euler step: move along the predicted velocity
steps.say: Step one runs the guided encoder and decoder, and moves the video latent seven point four percent of the way.
Step two runs the encoder alone. The expert jumps the actions to clean in one move, and the decoder is skipped. On the article's toy, with a fifty-fifty context, the reach lands between the mugs.
With eight steps and no shift, the action chunk gets clean enough, around a quarter of the way from the end, to resolve the choice by itself. The reach commits to one mug.
So where do errors come from? Sampling its own video, the arm misses by five point seven one centimetres on average.
Hand it the true future, noised to the same level, and the error drops to one point one four. The mistakes live in which future it imagines.

scenes.note: fifth overall; first among world action models
scenes.say: On a hundred and twenty simulated tasks: forty-six point two percent. Fifth overall, first among world action models. From one run.

scenes.credit: Runway's thread on X, sped up

steps.say: The launch also set it against a frontier agent on a pen cap. Praxis-1 is done in seconds, the agent takes minutes.
But that is a fine-tune on this robot against an agent running zero-shot. A gap in latency and cost, not capability.

scenes.title: Where it breaks
scenes.say: The article found three soft spots.

items.say: Its most common failure is reaching for an object that resembles the target.
Chunked execution means up to two point six nine seconds before a disturbance changes the motion.

items.text: Every robot is a full fine-tune
items.say: And every new robot is a full fine-tune of twenty-seven billion parameters.

scenes.text: The robot moves on a future the model has barely started imagining, so better imagination is where the errors live.
